pages.x: Pakistan was born in 1947 in two parts, 1,600 kilometres apart. The East, where Bengali was spoken, had more people, but the West held the power and the money. In 1952 students in Dhaka were shot for demanding that Bengali be a national language, on a day now kept around the world as International Mother Language Day.

In December 1970, weeks after a cyclone killed hundreds of thousands in the East while the government was slow to help, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's Awami League won a majority in all of Pakistan. The generals in the West would not let him take power. On 7 March 1971 he told a vast crowd in Dhaka that the struggle now was for freedom.

On the night of 25 March 1971 the Pakistani army struck, killing students, teachers and Hindus in Dhaka and arresting Mujib. Over nine months soldiers and their local allies killed civilians, raped hundreds of thousands of women and burned villages. Many call it a genocide.

Some ten million people fled over the border into India and lived in vast camps. Bengali fighters, the Mukti Bahini, trained in India and fought back. In August George Harrison and Ravi Shankar held the Concert for Bangladesh in New York, the first great charity concert, to raise money for the refugees.

In December Pakistan attacked Indian airfields, and India, led by Indira Gandhi, struck back in the East. In thirteen days Indian forces and the Mukti Bahini reached Dhaka, and on 16 December some 93,000 Pakistani soldiers surrendered, the largest surrender since the Second World War. Bangladesh was free.

Bangladesh, a nation founded on its language, is now home to over 170 million people. Mujib, called the father of the nation, was murdered in a coup in 1975. 16 December is kept as Victory Day, and the killings of 1971 are still remembered, and argued over, in both countries.
